title: dict()
summary: A hash map from hashable keys to values, with O(1) lookup and insertion order preserved.
description: The workhorse of Python. Since 3.7 insertion order is guaranteed by the language, not merely an implementation detail — which is what makes `dict.fromkeys` the order-preserving way to deduplicate.

raises.when: A key is unhashable, such as a list.

real_world_usage: Parsed JSON, configuration, lookup indexes, counting, and grouping records by a key.

common_mistakes.fix: Use d.get(key, default) when absence is expected. Keep d[key] for when absence is a bug you want reported.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a list as a key
common_mistakes.fix: Keys must be hashable. Convert to a tuple.

common_mistakes.mistake: Mutating a dict while iterating it
common_mistakes.fix: RuntimeError. Iterate over list(d) or build a new dict.

performance_notes: Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) average. Memory overhead is real — roughly 2–3x the payload — so a million small dicts is worth replacing with dataclasses with __slots__ or NamedTuples.
security_notes: Building dicts from untrusted keys is a memory vector, and pathological key sets can degrade hashing. Bound the number of distinct keys you will accept.
